entries.ef4f9ea9931d901c2251e07a7663f93e3f500821: <div sID="gen13173" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="141" osisID="Ps.141" sID="Ps.141"/> <div eID="gen13173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13174" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13175" type="x-p"/> David was in distress when he penned this psalm, pursued, it is most likely, by Saul, that violent man. Is any distressed? Let him pray; David did so, and had the comfort of it. I. He prays for God's favourable acceptance, <reference osisRef="Ps.141.1-Ps.141.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. For his powerful assistance, <reference osisRef="Ps.141.3-Ps.141.4">ver. 3, 4</reference>. III. That others might be instrumental of good to his soul, as he hoped to be to the souls of others, <reference osisRef="Ps.141.5-Ps.141.6">ver. 5, 6</reference>. IV. That he and his friends being now brought to the last extremity God would graciously appear for their relief and rescue, <reference osisRef="Ps.141.7-Ps.141.10">ver. 7-10</reference>. The mercy and grace of God are as necessary to us as they were to him, and therefore we should be humbly earnest for them in singing this psalm.
entries.15c0ed274cf74a6b87f6b5bc57895d6785511d88: <div eID="gen13175" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13174" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Fervent Supplications.</title> <div sID="gen13176" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , I cry unto thee: make haste unto me; give ear unto my voice, when I cry unto thee. <hi type="super">2</hi> Let my prayer be set forth before thee <hi type="italic">as</hi> incense; <hi type="italic">and</hi> the lifting up of my hands <hi type="italic">as</hi> the evening sacrifice. <hi type="super">3</hi> Set a watch, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , before my mouth; keep the door of my lips. <hi type="super">4</hi> Incline not my heart to <hi type="italic">any</hi> evil thing, to practise wicked works with men that work iniquity: and let me not eat of their dainties. <div eID="gen13176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13177" type="x-p"/> Mercy to accept what we do well, and grace to keep us from doing ill, are the two things which we are here taught by David's example to pray to God for. <div eID="gen13177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13178" type="x-p"/> I. David loved prayer, and he begs of God that his prayers might be heard and answered, <reference osisRef="Ps.141.1-Ps.141.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. <hi type="italic">David cried unto God.</hi> His crying denotes fervency in prayer; he prayed as one in earnest. His crying to God denotes faith and fixedness in prayer. And what did he desire as the success of his prayer? 1. That God would take cognizance of it: "<hi type="italic">Give ear to my voice;</hi> let me have a gracious audience." Those that cry in prayer may hope to be heard in prayer, not for their loudness, but their liveliness. 2. That he would visit him upon it: <hi type="italic">Make haste unto me.</hi> Those that know how to value God's gracious presence will be importunate for it and humbly impatient of delays. He that believes does not make haste, but he that prays may be earnest with God to make haste. 3. That he would be well pleased with him in it, well pleased with his <hi type="italic">praying</hi> and the <hi type="italic">lifting up of his hands in prayer,</hi> which denotes both the elevation and enlargement of his desire and the out-goings of his hope and expectation, the lifting up of the hand signifying the lifting up of the heart, and being used instead of lifting up the sacrifices which were heaved and waved before the Lord. Prayer is a spiritual sacrifice; it is the offering up of the soul, and its best affections, to God. Now he prays that this may be set forth and directed before God <hi type="italic">as the incense</hi> which was daily burnt upon the golden altar, and <hi type="italic">as the evening sacrifice,</hi> which he mentions rather than the morning sacrifice, perhaps because this was an evening prayer, or with an eye to Christ, who, in the evening of the world and in the evening of the day, was to offer up himself a sacrifice of atonement, and establish the spiritual sacrifices of acknowledgement, having abolished all the carnal ordinances of the law. Those that pray in faith may expect it will please God better than an ox or bullock. David was now banished from God's court, and could not attend the sacrifice and incense, and therefore begs that his prayer might be instead of them. Note, Prayer is of a sweet-smelling savour to God, as incense, which yet has no savour without fire; nor has prayer without the fire of holy love and fervour. <div eID="gen13178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13179" type="x-p"/> II. David was in fear of sin, and he begs of God that he might be kept from sin, knowing that his prayers would not be accepted unless he took care to watch against sin. We must be as earnest for God's grace in us as for his favour towards us. 1. He prays that he might not be surprised into any sinful words (<reference osisRef="Ps.141.3">v. 3</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Set a watch, O Lord! before my mouth,</hi> and, nature having made my lips to be a door to my words, let grace keep that door, that no word may be suffered to go out which may in any way tend to the dishonour of God or the hurt of others." Good men know the evil of tongue-sins, and how prone they are to them (when enemies are provoking we are in danger of carrying our resentment too far, and of speaking unadvisedly, as Moses did, though the meekest of men), and therefore they are earnest with God to prevent their speaking amiss, as knowing that no watchfulness or resolution of their own is sufficient for the governing of their tongues, much less of their hearts, without the special grace of God. We must <hi type="italic">keep our mouths as with a bridle;</hi> but that will not serve: we must pray to God to keep them. Nehemiah prayed to the Lord when he set a watch, and so must we, for without him the watchman walketh but in vain. 2. That he might not be inclined to any sinful practices (<reference osisRef="Ps.141.4">v. 4</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Incline not my heart to any evil thing;</hi> whatever inclination there is in me to sin, let it be not only restrained, but mortified, by divine grace." The example of those about us, and the provocations of those against us, are apt to stir up and draw out corrupt inclinations. We are ready to do as others do, and to think that if we have received injuries we may return them; and therefore we have need to pray that we may never be left to ourselves to practise any wicked work, either in confederacy with or in opposition to the <hi type="italic">men that work iniquity.</hi> While we live in such an evil world, and carry about with us such evil hearts, we have need to pray that we may neither be drawn in by any allurement nor driven on by any provocation to do any sinful thing. 3. That he might not be ensnared by any sinful pleasures: "<hi type="italic">Let me not eat of their dainties.</hi> Let me not join with them in their feasts and sports, lest thereby I be inveigled into their sins." <hi type="italic">Better is a dinner of herbs,</hi> out of the way of temptation, than a <hi type="italic">stalled ox</hi> in it. Sinners pretend to find dainties in sin. <hi type="italic">Stolen waters are sweet;</hi> forbidden fruit is pleasant to the eye. But those that consider how soon the dainties of sin will turn into wormwood and gall, how certainly it will, at last, <hi type="italic">bite like a serpent</hi> and <hi type="italic">sting like an adder,</hi> will dread those dainties, and pray to God by his providence to take them out of their sight, and by his grace to turn them against them. Good men will pray even against the sweets of sin.
entries.446371a8002cbc19910422e38a0b00996081ee47: <div eID="gen13179" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Reproofs of the Righteous; Complaints and Petitions.</title> <div sID="gen13180" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> Let the righteous smite me; <hi type="italic">it shall be</hi> a kindness: and let him reprove me; <hi type="italic">it shall be</hi> an excellent oil, <hi type="italic">which</hi> shall not break my head: for yet my prayer also <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> in their calamities. <hi type="super">6</hi> When their judges are overthrown in stony places, they shall hear my words; for they are sweet. <hi type="super">7</hi> Our bones are scattered at the grave's mouth, as when one cutteth and cleaveth <hi type="italic">wood</hi> upon the earth. <hi type="super">8</hi> But mine eyes <hi type="italic">are</hi> unto thee, <hi type="small-caps">O God</hi> the Lord: in thee is my trust; leave not my soul destitute. <hi type="super">9</hi> Keep me from the snares <hi type="italic">which</hi> they have laid for me, and the gins of the workers of iniquity. <hi type="super">10</hi> Let the wicked fall into their own nets, whilst that I withal escape. <div eID="gen13180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13181" type="x-p"/> Here, I. David desires to be told of his faults. His enemies reproached him with that which was false, which he could not but complain of; yet, at the same time, he desired his friends would reprove him for that which was really amiss in him, particularly if there was any thing that gave the least colour to those reproaches (<reference osisRef="Ps.141.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">let the righteous smite me; it shall be a kindness.</hi> The <hi type="italic">righteous God</hi> (so some); "I will welcome the rebukes of his providence, and be so far from quarrelling with them that I will receive them as tokens of love and improve them as means of grace, and will pray for those that are the instruments of my trouble." But it is commonly taken for the reproofs given by righteous men; and it best becomes those that are themselves righteous to reprove the unrighteousness of others, and from them reproof will be best taken. But if the reproof be just, though the reprover be not so, we must make a good use of it and learn obedience by it. We are here taught how to receive the reproofs of the righteous and wise. 1. We must desire to be reproved for whatever is amiss in us, or is done amiss by us: "Lord, put it into the heart of the righteous to smite me and reprove me. If my own heart does not <hi type="italic">smite me,</hi> as it ought, let my friend do it; let me never fall under that dreadful judgment of being let alone in sin." 2. We must account it a piece of friendship. We must not only bear it patiently, but take it as a kindness; for <hi type="italic">reproofs of instruction are the way of life</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.6.23">Prov. vi. 23</reference>), are means of good to us, to bring us to repentance for the sins we have committed, and to prevent relapses into sin. Though reproofs cut, it is in order to a cure, and therefore they are much more desirable than the kisses of an enemy (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.6">Prov. xxvii. 6</reference>) or the song of fools, <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.5">Eccl. vii. 5</reference>. David blessed God for Abigail's seasonable admonition, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.32">1 Sam. xxv. 32</reference>. 3. We must reckon ourselves helped and healed by it: It <hi type="italic">shall be as an excellent oil</hi> to a wound, to mollify it and close it up; <hi type="italic">it shall not break my head,</hi> as some reckon it to do, who could as well bear to have their heads broken as to be told of their faults; but, says David, "I am not of that mind; it is my sin that has broken my head, that has broken my bones, <reference osisRef="Ps.51.8">Ps. li. 8</reference>. The reproof is an excellent oil, to cure the bruises sin has given me. It shall not <hi type="italic">break my head,</hi> if it may but help to break my heart." 4. We must requite the kindness of those that deal thus faithfully, thus friendly with us, at least by our <hi type="italic">prayers for them in their calamities,</hi> and hereby we must show that we take it kindly. Dr. Hammond gives quite another reading of this verse: "<hi type="italic">Reproach will bruise me that am righteous, and rebuke me; but that poisonous oil shall not break my head</hi> (shall not destroy me, shall not do me the mischief intended), <hi type="italic">for yet my prayer shall be in their mischiefs,</hi> that God would preserve me from them, and my prayer shall not be in vain." <div eID="gen13181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13182" type="x-p"/> II. David hopes his persecutors will, some time or other, bear to be told of their faults, as he was willing to be told of his (<reference osisRef="Ps.141.6">v. 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">When their judges</hi>" (Saul and his officers who judged and condemned David, and would themselves be sole judges) "<hi type="italic">are overthrown in stony places,</hi> among the rocks in the wilderness, then <hi type="italic">they shall hear my words, for they are sweet.</hi>" Some think this refers to the relentings that were in Saul's breast when he said, with tears, <hi type="italic">Is this thy voice, my son David?</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.16">1 Sam. xxiv. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.21">xxvi. 21</reference>. Or we may take it more generally: even judges, great as they are, may come to be overthrown. Those that make the greatest figure in this world do not always meet with level smooth ways through it. And those that slighted the word of God before will relish it, and be glad of it, when they are in affliction, for that opens the ear to instruction. When the world is bitter the word is sweet. Oppressed innocency cannot gain a hearing with those that live in pomp and pleasure, but when they come to be overthrown themselves they will have more compassionate thoughts of the afflicted. <div eID="gen13182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13183" type="x-p"/> III. David complains of the great extremity to which he and his friends were reduced (<reference osisRef="Ps.141.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">Our bones are scattered at the grave's mouth,</hi> out of which they are thrown up, so long have we been dead, or into which they are ready to be thrown, so near are we to the pit; and they are as little regarded as chips among the hewers of wood, which are thrown in neglected heaps: <hi type="italic">As one that cuts and cleaves the earth</hi> (so some read it), alluding to the ploughman who tears the earth in pieces with his plough-share, <reference osisRef="Ps.129.3">Ps. cxxix. 3</reference>. <hi type="italic">Can these dry bones live?</hi> <div eID="gen13183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13184" type="x-p"/> IV. David casts himself upon God, and depends upon him for deliverance: "<hi type="italic">But my eyes are unto thee</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.141.8">v. 8</reference>); for, when the case is ever so deplorable, thou canst redress all the grievances. From thee I expect relief, bad as things are, and in <hi type="italic">thee is my trust.</hi>" Those that have their eye towards God may have their hopes in him. <div eID="gen13184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13185" type="x-p"/> V. He prays that God would succour and relieve him as his necessity required. 1. That he would comfort him: "<hi type="italic">Leave not my soul desolate and destitute;</hi> still let me see where my help is." 2. That he would prevent the designs of his enemies against him (<reference osisRef="Ps.141.9">v. 9</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Keep me from</hi> being taken in <hi type="italic">the snare they have laid for me;</hi> give me to discover it and to evade it." Be the gin placed with ever so much subtlety, God can and will secure his people from being taken in it. 3. That God would, in justice, turn the designs of his enemies upon themselves, and, in mercy, deliver him from being ruined by them (<reference osisRef="Ps.141.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">let the wicked fall into their own net,</hi> the net which, intentionally, they procured for me, but which, meritoriously, they prepared for themselves. <hi type="italic">Nec lex est justioir ulla quam necis artifices arte perire sua—No law can be more just than that the architects of destruction should perish by their own contrivances.</hi> All that are bound over to God's justice are held in the cords of their own iniquity. But let me at the same time obtain a discharge. The entangling and ensnaring of the wicked sometimes prove the escape and enlargement of the righteous.  <chapter eID="Ps.141"/> <div eID="gen13185" type="x-p"/>

entries.45a6c9acccf5f17ae25930d8da86b42b6db7b371: <chapter n="141" osisID="Ps.141" sID="Ps.141"/><div eID="gen10878" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7096"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 141</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.141.1-Ps.141.10">Psa 141:1-10</reference>. This Psalm evinces its authorship as the preceding, by its structure and the character of its contents. It is a prayer for deliverance from sins to which affliction tempted him, and from the enemies who caused it.</title> <div sID="gen10879" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Ps.141"/>

entries.9550c435272509154781747e46e3ec90a1b8f9de: <div eID="gen23380" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen23381" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23382" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23382" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23381" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23383" type="x-p"/> The psalmist prays that his devotions may be accepted, <reference osisRef="Psa.141.1">Psa 141:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.141.2">Psa 141:2</reference>. That he may be enabled so to watch that he do not offend with his tongue; and that he may be preserved from wickedness, <reference osisRef="Psa.141.3">Psa 141:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.141.4">Psa 141:4</reference>. His willingness to receive reproof, <reference osisRef="Psa.141.5">Psa 141:5</reference>. He complains of disasters, <reference osisRef="Psa.141.6">Psa 141:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.141.7">Psa 141:7</reference>. His trust in God, and prayer against his enemies, <reference osisRef="Psa.141.8-Psa.141.10">Psa 141:8-10</reference>. <div eID="gen23383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23384" type="x-p"/> This Psalm is generally attributed to David, and considered to have been composed during his persecution by Saul. Some suppose that he made it at the time that he formed the resolution to go to Achish, king of Gath; see 1 Samuel 26: It is generally thought to be an evening prayer, and has long been used as such in the service of the Greek Church. It is in several places very obscure. <div eID="gen23384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23385" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen23385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23386" type="x-p"/> Lord, I cry unto thee - Many of David's Psalms begin with complaints; but they are not those of habitual plaint and peevishness. He was in frequent troubles and difficulties, and he always sought help in God. He ever appears in earnest; at no time is there any evidence that the devotion of David was formal. He prayed, meditated, supplicated, groaned, cried, and even roared, as he tells us, for the disquietude of his soul. He had speedy answers; for he had much faith, and was always in earnest.
entries.19ac1ee81ff6a32c2d328d989136823fe678392e: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen23386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23387" type="x-p"/> As incense - Incense was offered every morning and evening before the Lord, on the golden altar, before the veil of the sanctuary. <reference osisRef="Exo.29.39">Exo 29:39</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Num.28.4">Num 28:4</reference>. <div eID="gen23387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23388" type="x-p"/> As the evening sacrifice - This was a burnt-offering, accompanied with flour and salt. But it does not appear that David refers to any sacrifice, for he uses not זבח zebach, which is almost universally used for a slaughtered animal; but מנחה minchah, which is generally taken for a gratitude-offering or unbloody sacrifice. The literal translation of the passage is, "Let my prayer be established for incense before thy faces; and the lifting up of my hands for the evening oblation." The psalmist appears to have been at this time at a distance from the sanctuary, and therefore could not perform the Divine worship in the way prescribed by the law. What could he do? Why, as he could not worship according to the letter of the law, he will worship God according to the spirit; then prayer is accepted in the place of incense; and the lifting up of his hands, in gratitude and self-dedication to God, is accepted in the place of the evening minchah or oblation. Who can deplore the necessity that obliged the psalmist to worship God in this way?
entries.a2706ee644c493005259dd42cd54aa8e8707b043: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen23388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23389" type="x-p"/> Set a watch, O Lord, before my mouth - While there are so many spies on my actions and words, I have need to be doubly guarded, that my enemies may have no advantage against me. Some think the prayer is against impatience; but if he were now going to Gath, it is more natural to suppose that he was praying to be preserved from dishonoring the truth, and from making sinful concessions in a heathen land; and at a court where, from his circumstances, it was natural to suppose he might be tempted to apostasy by the heathen party. The following verse seems to support this opinion.
entries.8ee2615c847f68260b0f39189fd5c8a913b02328: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen23389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23390" type="x-p"/> Let me eat not of their dainties - This may refer either to eating things forbidden by the law; or to the partaking in banquets or feasts in honor of idols.
entries.0c2622abacc2c9cf9c5717e4517d43ba5388ba2a: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen23390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23391" type="x-p"/> Let the righteous smite me - This verse is extremely difficult in the original. The following translation, in which the Syriac, Vulgate, Septuagint, Ethiopic, and Arabic nearly agree, appears to me to be the best: "Let the righteous chastise me in mercy, and instruct me: but let not the oil of the wicked anoint my head. It shall not adorn (יני yani, from נוה navah) my head; for still my prayer shall be against their wicked works." <div eID="gen23391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23392" type="x-p"/> The oil of the wicked may here mean his smooth flattering speeches; and the psalmist intimates that he would rather suffer the cutting reproof of the righteous than the oily talk of the flatterer. If this were the case, how few are there now-a-days of his mind! On referring to Bishop Horsley, I find his translation is something similar to my own: - <div eID="gen23392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23393" type="x-p"/> Let the just one smite me, let the pious remove me. <div eID="gen23393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23394" type="x-p"/> Let not the ointment of the impious anoint my head. <div eID="gen23394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23395" type="x-p"/> But still I will intrude in their calamities.
entries.bc69f105679f17e24a6134bd43061569caa2bd65: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen23395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23396" type="x-p"/> When their judges are overthrown in stony places - בידי סלע biyedey sela, "In the hands of the rock." Does this rock signify a strong or fortified place; and its hands the garrison which have occupied it, by whom these judges were overthrown? If we knew the occasion on which this Psalm was made, we might be the better able to understand the allusions in the text. <div eID="gen23396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23397" type="x-p"/> They shall hear my words; for they are sweet - Some think there is here an allusion to David's generous treatment of Saul in the cave of En-gedi, and afterwards at the hill of Hachilah, in this verse, which might be translated: "Their judges have been dismissed in the rocky places; and have heard my words, that they were sweet." Or perhaps there may be a reference to the death of Saul and his sons, and the very disastrous defeat of the Israelites at Gilboa. If so, the seventh verse will lose its chief difficulty, Our bones are scattered at the grave's mouth; but if we take them as referring to the slaughter of the priests at Nob, then, in stead of translating לפי שאול lephi sheol, at the grave's mouth, we may translate at the command of Saul; and then the verse will point out the manner in which those servants of the Lord were massacred; Doeg cut them in pieces; hewed them down as one cleaveth wood. Some understand all this of the cruel usage of the captives in Babylon. I could add other conjectures, and contend for my own; but they are all too vague to form a just ground for decided opinion.
entries.8672b245fd5354c196f85e5708ffa8114a7e6897: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen23397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23398" type="x-p"/> But mine eyes are unto thee - In all times, in all places, on all occasions, I will cleave unto the Lord, and put my whole confidence in him.
entries.2a77ca197cc1d503b66f94f9e9dd16dbb46bddb1: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen23398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23399" type="x-p"/> Let the wicked fall into their own nets - This is generally the case; those who lay snares for others fall into them themselves. Harm watch, harm catch, says the old adage. How many cases have occurred where the spring guns that have been set for thieves have shot some of the family! I have known some dismal cases of this kind, where some of the most amiable lives have been sacrificed to this accursed machine. <div eID="gen23399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23400" type="x-p"/> Whilst - I withal escape - They alone are guilty; they alone spread the nets and gins; I am innocent, and God will cause me to escape.  <chapter eID="Ps.141"/> <div eID="gen23400" type="x-p"/>

entries.cc9551ac0e2c3ad9c93f85e14ff1caa043e52805: <div eID="gen10294" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Evening Psalm in the Times of Absalom</title> <div sID="gen10295" type="x-p"/> The four Psalms, <reference osisRef="Ps.140.1-Ps.140.13">Psa 140:1-13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.141.1-Ps.141.10">Psa 141:1-10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.142.1-Ps.142.7">Psa 142:1-7</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Ps.143.1-Ps.143.12">Psa 143:1-12</reference>, are interwoven with one another in many ways (<hi type="italic">Symbolae</hi>, pp. 67f.). The following passages are very similar, viz., <reference osisRef="Ps.140.7">Psa 140:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.141.1">Psa 141:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.142.2">Psa 142:2</reference>, and Psa 143:1. Just as the poet complains in <reference osisRef="Ps.142.4">Psa 142:4</reference>, “when my spirit veils itself within me,” so too in <reference osisRef="Ps.143.4">Psa 143:4</reference>; as he prays in Ps 142:8, “Oh bring my soul out of prison,” so in <reference osisRef="Ps.143.11">Psa 143:11</reference>, “bring my soul out of distress,” where צרה takes the place of the metaphorical מסגר. Besides these, compare <reference osisRef="Ps.140.5-Ps.140.6">Psa 140:5-6</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.141.9">Psa 141:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.142.7">Psa 142:7</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.143.9">Psa 143:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.140.3">Psa 140:3</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.141.5">Psa 141:5</reference>, רעות; Ps 140:14 with Ps 142:8; <reference osisRef="Ps.142.4">Psa 142:4</reference> with Psa 143:8. <div eID="gen10295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10296" type="x-p"/> The right understanding of the Psalm depends upon the right understanding of the situation. Since it is inscribed לדוד, it is presumably a situation corresponding to the history of David, out of the midst of which the Psalm is composed, either by David himself or by some one else who desired to give expression in Davidic strains to David’s mood when in this situation. For the gleaning of Davidic Psalms which we find in the last two Books of the Psalter is for the most part derived from historical works in which these Psalms, in some instances only free reproductions of the feelings of David with respect to old Davidic models, adorned the historic narrative. The Psalm before us adorned the history of the time of the persecution by Absalom. At that time David was driven out of Jerusalem, and consequently cut off from the sacrificial worship of God upon Zion; and our Psalm is an evening hymn of one of those troublous days. The ancient church, even prior to the time of Gregory (<hi type="italic">Constitutiones Apostolicae</hi>, ii. 59), had chosen it for its evening hymn, just as it had chosen <reference osisRef="Ps.63.1-Ps.63.11">Psa 63:1-11</reference> for its morning hymn. Just as <reference osisRef="Ps.63.1-Ps.63.11">Psa 63:1-11</reference> was called ὁ ὀρθρινός (<hi type="italic">ibid</hi>. 8:37), so this Psalm, as being the Vesper Psalm, was called ὁ ἐπιλύχνιος (vid., 8:35).
entries.6c2a82142ac37941f82616150e7777c2ede3274a: <reference osisRef="Ps.141.1-Ps.141.2">Psa 141:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen10296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10297" type="x-p"/> The very beginning of <reference osisRef="Ps.141.1-Ps.141.10">Psa 141:1-10</reference> is more after the manner of David than really Davidic; for instead of <hi type="italic">haste thee to me</hi>, David always says, <hi type="italic">haste thee for my help</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.20">Psa 22:20</reference>; 38:23; Psa 40:14. The לך that is added to בּקראי (as in <reference osisRef="Ps.4.2">Psa 4:2</reference>) is to be explained, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.57.3">Psa 57:3</reference> : when I call to Thee, i.e., when I call Thee, who art now far from me, to me. The general cry for help is followed in <reference osisRef="Ps.141.2">Psa 141:2</reference> by a petition for the answering of his prayer. Luther has given an excellent rendering: Let my prayer avail to Thee as an offering of incense; the lifting up of my hands, as an evening sacrifice (<hi type="italic">Mein Gebet müsse fur dir tügen wie ein Reuchopffer, Meine Hende auffheben, wie ein Abendopffer</hi>). תּכּון is the <hi type="italic">fut. Niph.</hi> of כּוּן, and signifies properly to be set up, and to be established, or reflexive: to place and arrange or prepare one’s self, <reference osisRef="Amos.4.12">Amo 4:12</reference>; then to continue, e.g., <reference osisRef="Ps.101.7">Psa 101:7</reference>; therefore, either let it place itself, let it appear, <hi type="italic">sistat se</hi>, or better: let it stand, continue, i.e., let my prayer find acceptance, recognition with Thee קטרת, and the lifting up of my hands מנחת־ערב. Expositors say that this in both instances is the <hi type="italic">comparatio decurtata</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.11.1">Psa 11:1</reference> and elsewhere: as an incense-offering, as an evening <hi type="italic">mincha</hi>. But the poet purposely omits the כּ of the comparison. He wishes that God may be pleased to regard his prayer as sweet-smelling smoke or as incense, just as this was added to the <hi type="italic">azcara</hi> of the meal-offering, and gave it, in its ascending perfume, the direction upward to God,<note placement="foot">It is not the priestly קטרת תּמיד, i.e., the daily morning and evening incense-offering upon the golden altar of the holy place, <reference osisRef="Exod.30.8">Exo 30:8</reference>, that is meant (since it is a non-priest who is speaking, according to Hitzig, of course John Hyrcanus), but rather, as also in <reference osisRef="Isa.1.13">Isa 1:13</reference>, the incense of the <hi type="italic">azcara</hi> of the meal-offering which the priest burnt (הקטיר) upon the altar; the incense (<reference osisRef="Isa.66.3">Isa 66:3</reference>) was entirely consumed, and not merely a handful taken from it.</note> and that He may be pleased to regard the lifting up of his hands (משׂאת, the construct with the reduplication given up, from משּׂאת, or even, after the form מתּנת, from משּׂאה, here not <hi type="italic">oblatio</hi>, but according to the phrase נשׂא כפּים ידים, <hi type="italic">elevatio</hi>, Jdg 20:38, Jdg 20:40, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.28.2">Psa 28:2</reference>, and frequently) as an evening <hi type="italic">mincha</hi>, just as it was added to the evening <hi type="italic">tamı̂d</hi> according to <reference osisRef="Exod.29.38-Exod.29.42">Exo 29:38-42</reference>, and concluded the work of the service of the day.<note placement="foot">The reason of it is this, that the evening <hi type="italic">mincha</hi> is oftener mentioned than the morning <hi type="italic">mincha</hi> (see, however, 2Ki 3:20). The whole burnt-offering of the morning and the meat-offering of the evening (2Ki 16:15; 1Ki 18:29, 1Ki 18:36) are the beginning and close of the daily principal service; whence, according to the example of the <hi type="italic">usus</hi> <hi type="italic">loquendi</hi> in <reference osisRef="Dan.9.21">Dan 9:21</reference>; Ezr 9:4., later on <hi type="italic">mincha</hi> directly signifies the afternoon or evening.</note>
entries.c7b488bacfb4ead01427ea755bc92e282d40f936: <reference osisRef="Ps.141.3-Ps.141.4">Psa 141:3-4</reference> <div eID="gen10297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10298" type="x-p"/> The prayer now begins to be particularized, and that in the first instance as a petition fore the grace of silence, calling to mind old Davidic passages like <reference osisRef="Ps.39.2">Psa 39:2</reference>; Psa 34:14. The situation of David, the betrayed one, requires caution in speaking; and the consciousness of having sinned, not indeed against the rebels, but against God, who would not visit him thus without his deserving it, stood in the way of any outspoken self-vindication. In <hi type="italic">pone custodiam ori meo</hi> שׁמרה is ἅπ. λεγ., after the infinitive form דּבקה, עזבה, עצמה. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.141.3">Psa 141:3</reference></hi> דּל is ἅπ. λεγ. for דּלת; cf. “doors of the mouth” in Mic 7:5, and πύλαι στόματος in Euripides. נצּרה might be <hi type="italic">imper. Kal</hi>: keep I pray, with <hi type="italic">Dag. dirimens</hi> as in Pro 4:13. But נצר על is not in use; and also as the parallel word to שׁמרה, which likewise has the appearance of being imperative, נצּרה is explicable as regards its pointing by a comparison of יקּהה in <reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Gen 49:10</reference>, דּבּרה in <reference osisRef="Deut.33.3">Deu 33:3</reference>, and קרבה in Psa 73:28. The prayer for the grace of silence is followed in <reference osisRef="Ps.141.4">Psa 141:4</reference> by a prayer for the breaking off of all fellowship with the existing rulers. By a flight of irony they are called אישׁים, lords, in the sense of בּני אישׁ, <reference osisRef="Ps.4.3">Psa 4:3</reference> (cf. the Spanish <hi type="italic">hidalgos</hi> = <hi type="italic">hijos d'algo</hi>, sons of somebody). The evil thing (רע | דּבר, with <hi type="italic">Pasek</hi> between the two ר, as in Num 7:13; <reference osisRef="Deut.7.1">Deu 7:1</reference> between the two מ, and in <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.3">1Ch 22:3</reference> between the two )ל, to which Jahve may be pleased never to incline his heart (תּט, <hi type="italic">fut. apoc.</hi> <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. as in <reference osisRef="Ps.27.9">Psa 27:9</reference>), is forthwith more particularly designated: <hi type="italic">perpetrare facinora maligne cum dominis, etc.</hi> עללות of great achievements in the sense of infamous deeds, also occurs in <reference osisRef="Ps.14.1">Psa 14:1</reference>; Psa 99:8. Here, however, we have the <hi type="italic">Hithpo</hi>. התעלל, which, with the accusative of the object עללות, signifies: wilfully to make such actions the object of one’s acting (cf. Arab. <hi type="italic">ta‛allala b - 'l - š'</hi>, to meddle with any matter, to amuse, entertain one’s self with a thing). The expression is made to express disgust as strongly as possible; this poet is fond of glaring colouring in his language. In the dependent passage <hi type="italic">neve eorum vescar cupediis, </hi>לחם is used poetically for אכל, and בּ is the partitive <hi type="italic">Beth</hi>, as in Job 21:25. מנעמּים is another hapaxlegomenon, but as being a designation of dainties (from נעם, to be mild, tender, pleasant), it may not have been an unusual word. It is a well-known thing that usurpers revel in the <hi type="italic">cuisine</hi> and cellars of those whom they have driven away.
entries.ee285e026a34b27d68af9ea39e3aeeb4a8816d3b: <reference osisRef="Ps.141.5-Ps.141.7">Psa 141:5-7</reference> <div eID="gen10298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10299" type="x-p"/> Thus far the Psalm is comparatively easy of exposition; but now it becomes difficult, yet not hopelessly so. David, thoroughly conscious of his sins against God and of his imperfection as a monarch, says, in opposition to the abuse which he is now suffering, that he would gladly accept any friendly reproof: “let a righteous man smite in kindness and reprove me - head-oil (i.e., oil upon the head, to which such reproof is likened) shall my head not refuse.” So we render it, following the accents, and not as Hupfeld, Kurtz, and Hitzig do: “if a righteous man smites me, it is love; if he reproves me, an anointing of the head is it unto me;” in connection with which the designation of the subject with היא would be twice wanting, which is more than is admissible. צדּיק stands here as an abstract substantive: the righteous man, whoever he may be, in antithesis, namely, to the rebels and to the people who have joined them. Amyraldus, Maurer, and Hengstenberg understand it of God; but it only occurs of God as an attribute, and never as a direct appellation. חסד, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.31.3">Jer 31:3</reference>, is equivalent to בּחסד, <hi type="italic">cum benignitate = benigne</hi>. What is meant is, as in <reference osisRef="Job.6.14">Job 6:14</reference>, what Paul (<reference osisRef="Gal.6.1">Gal 6:1</reference>) styles πνεῦμα πραΰ́τητος. and הלם, <hi type="italic">tundere</hi>, is used of the strokes of earnest but well-meant reproof, which is called “the blows of a friend” in Pro 27:6. Such reproof shall be to him as head-oil (<reference osisRef="Ps.23.5">Psa 23:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.133.2">Psa 133:2</reference>), which his head does not despise. יני, written defectively for יניא, like ישּׁי, in <reference osisRef="Ps.55.16">Psa 55:16</reference>, אבי, 1Ki 21:29 and frequently; הניא (root נא, Arab. <hi type="italic">n'</hi>, with the nasal <hi type="italic">n</hi>, which also expresses the negation in the Indo-Germanic languages) here signifies to deny, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.33.10">Psa 33:10</reference> to bring to nought, to destroy. On the other hand, the lxx renders μὴ λιπανάτω τὴν κεφαλήν μου, which is also followed by the Syriac and Jerome, perhaps after the Arabic <hi type="italic">nawiya</hi>, to become or to be fat, which is, however, altogether foreign to the Aramaic, and is, moreover, only used of fatness of the body, and in fact of camels. The meaning of the figure is this: well-meant reproof shall be acceptable and spiritually useful to him. The confirmation כּי־עוד וגו follows, which is enigmatical both in meaning and expression. This עוד is the cipher of a whole clause, and the following ו is related to this עוד as the <hi type="italic">Waw</hi> that introduces the apodosis, not to כּי as in <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.20">2Ch 24:20</reference>, since no progression and connection is discernible if כי is taken as a subordinating <hi type="italic">quia</hi>. We interpret thus: <hi type="italic">for it is still so</hi> (the matter still stands thus), that my prayer is against their wickednesses; i.e., that I use no weapon but that of prayer against these, therefore let me always be in that spiritual state of mind which is alive to well-meant reproof. Mendelssohn’s rendering is similar: I still pray, whilst they practise infamy. On עוד ו cf. Zec 8:20 עוד אשׁר (vid., Köhler), and <reference osisRef="Prov.24.27">Pro 24:27</reference> אחר ו. He who has prayed God in <reference osisRef="Ps.141.3">Psa 141:3</reference> to set a watch upon his mouth is dumb in the presence of those who now have dominion, and seeks to keep himself clear of their sinful doings, whereas he willingly allows himself to be chastened by the righteous; and the more silent he is towards the world (see <reference osisRef="Amos.5.13">Amo 5:13</reference>), the more constant is he in his intercourse with God. But there will come a time when those who now behave as lords shall fall a prey to the revenge of the people who have been misled by them; and on the other hand, the confession of the salvation, and of the order of the salvation, of God, that has hitherto been put to silence, will again be able to make itself freely heard, and find a ready hearing. <div eID="gen10299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10300" type="x-p"/> As <reference osisRef="Ps.141.6">Psa 141:6</reference> says, the new rulers fall a prey to the indignation of the people and are thrown down the precipices, whilst the people, having again come to their right mind, obey the words of David and find them pleasant and beneficial (vid., <reference osisRef="Prov.15.26">Pro 15:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.16.24">Pro 16:24</reference>). נשׁמטוּ is to be explained according to 2Ki 9:33. The casting of persons down from the rock was not an unusual mode of execution (<reference osisRef="2Chr.25.12">2Ch 25:12</reference>). ידי־סלע are the sides (<reference osisRef="Ps.140.6">Psa 140:6</reference>; Jdg 11:26) of the rock, after which the expression ἐχόμενα πέτρας of the lxx, which has been misunderstood by Jerome, is intended to be understood;<note placement="foot">Beda Pieringer in his <hi type="italic">Psalterium Romana Lyra Radditum</hi> (Ratisbonae 1859) interprets κατεπόθησαν ἐχόμενα πέτρας οἱ κραταιοὶ τὐτῶν, <hi type="italic">absorpti</hi>, i.e., <hi type="italic">operti sunt loco ad petram pertinente signiferi turpis consilii eorum</hi>.</note> they are therefore the sides of the rock conceived of as it were as the hands of the body of rock, if we are not rather with Böttcher to compare the expressions בּידי and על־ידי construed with verbs of abandoning and casting down, <reference osisRef="Lam.1.14">Lam 1:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.16.11">Job 16:11</reference>, and frequently. In <reference osisRef="Ps.141.7">Psa 141:7</reference> there follows a further statement of the issue on the side of David and his followers: <hi type="italic">instar findentis et secantis terram</hi> (בּקע with <hi type="italic">Beth</hi>, elsewhere in the hostile signification of <hi type="italic">irrumpere</hi>) <hi type="italic">dispersa sunt ossa nostra ad ostium</hi> (לפי as in <reference osisRef="Prov.8.3">Pro 8:3</reference>) <hi type="italic">orci</hi>; Symmachus: ὥσπερ γεωργὸς ὅταν ῥήσσῃ τὴν τὴν, οὕτως ἐσκορπίσθη τὰ ὀστᾶ ἡμῶν εἰς στόμα ᾅδου; Quinta: ὡς καλλιεργῶν καὶ σκάπτων ἐν τῇ γῇ κ. τ. λ. Assuming the very extreme, it is a look of hope into the future: should his bones and the bones of his followers be even scattered about the mouth of Sheôl (cf. the Syrian picture of Sheôl: “the dust upon its threshold <hi type="italic">‛al - escûfteh ,” Deutsche Morgenländ. Zeitschrift</hi>, xx. 513), their soul below, their bones above - it would nevertheless be only as when on in ploughing cleaves the earth; i.e., they do not lie there in order that they may continue lying, but that they may rise up anew, as the seed that is sown sprouts up out of the upturned earth. lxx <hi type="italic">Codd. Vat. et Sinait</hi>. τὰ ὀστᾶ ἡμῶν, beside which, however, is found the reading αὐτῶν (<hi type="italic">Cod. Alex.</hi> by a second hand, and the Syriac, Arabic, and Aethiopic versions), as Böttcher also, <hi type="italic">pro ineptissimo utcunque</hi>, thinks עצמינו must be read, understanding this, according to <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.12">2Ch 25:12</reference> <hi type="italic">extrem</hi>., of the mangled bodies of those cast down from the rock. We here discern the hope of a resurrection, if not directly, at least (cf. Oehler in Herzog’s <hi type="italic">Real-Encyclopädie</hi>, concluding volume, S. 422) as am emblem of victory in spite of having succumbed. That which authorizes this interpretation lies in the figure of the husbandman, and in the conditional clause (<reference osisRef="Ps.141.8">Psa 141:8</reference>), which leads to the true point of the comparison; for as a complaint concerning a defeat that had been suffered: “so are our bones scattered for the mouth of the grave (in order to be swallowed up by it),” <reference osisRef="Ps.141.7">Psa 141:7</reference>, would be alien and isolated with respect to what precedes and what follows.
entries.73b86b076dba42c119b46f4349ea498ba4f6be9b: <reference osisRef="Ps.141.8-Ps.141.10">Psa 141:8-10</reference> <div eID="gen10300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10301" type="x-p"/> If <reference osisRef="Ps.141.7">Psa 141:7</reference> is not merely an expression of the complaint, but at the same time of hope, we now have no need to give the כּי the adversative sense of <hi type="italic">imo</hi>, but we may leave it its most natural confirmatory signification <hi type="italic">namque</hi>. From this point the Psalm gradually dies away in strains comparatively easy to be understood and in perfect keeping with the situation. In connection with <reference osisRef="Ps.141.8">Psa 141:8</reference> one is reminded of <reference osisRef="Ps.25.15">Psa 25:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.31.2">Psa 31:2</reference>; with Psa 141:9., of <reference osisRef="Ps.7.16">Psa 7:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.69.23">Psa 69:23</reference>, and other passages. In “pour not out (תּער with sharpened vowel instead of תּער, Ges. §75, rem. 8) my soul,” ערה, <hi type="italic">Piel</hi>, is equivalent to the <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. הערה in Isa 53:12. ידי פח are as it were the hands of the seizing and capturing snare; and יקשׂוּ לּי is virtually a genitive: <hi type="italic">qui insidias tendunt mihi</hi>, since one cannot say יקשׁ פח, <hi type="italic">ponere laqueum</hi>. מכמרים, nets, in <reference osisRef="Ps.141.10">Psa 141:10</reference> is another hapaxlegomenon; the <hi type="italic">enallage numeri</hi> is as in <reference osisRef="Ps.62.5">Psa 62:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.2.8">Isa 2:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.5.23">Isa 5:23</reference>, - the singular that slips in refers what is said of the many to each individual in particular. The plural מקשׁות for מקשׁים, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.6">Psa 18:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.64.6">Psa 64:6</reference>, also occurs only here. יחד is to be explained as in 4:9: it is intended to express the coincidence of the overthrow of the enemies and the going forth free of the persecuted one. With יחד אנכי the poet gives prominence to his simultaneous, distinct destiny: <hi type="italic">simul ego dum</hi> (עד as in <reference osisRef="Job.8.21">Job 8:21</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Job.1.18">Job 1:18</reference>) <hi type="italic">praetereo h.e. evado</hi>. The inverted position of the כּי in <reference osisRef="Ps.18.10-Ps.18.12">Psa 18:10-12</reference> may be compared; with <reference osisRef="Ps.120.7">Psa 120:7</reference> and 2Ki 2:14, however (where instead of אף־הוּא it is with Thenius to be read אפוא), the case is different.  <chapter eID="Ps.141"/> <div eID="gen10301" type="x-p"/>

entries.d948afd5f948bfa72ea8b0fd3883fd7ce7ee467a:
PSALM 141
Whatever may have been the immediate cause pressing David to pray in the manner he does in this Psalm,
Many commentators are strongly of opinion, that this Psalm was written as a memorial of that very interesting scene in the life of David, recorded in 1 Samuel 24, relating to his generous treatment of Saul. Though he had an opportunity of putting that his cruel persecutor to death in the cave of En-gedi, yet he spared his life, only cutting off his skirt, and not suffering his followers to touch him; and when Saul had gone out of the cave, David going out after him, remonstrated with him from some distance in the gentlest and most respectful language in regard to the injustice of his conduct towards him. It is thought that the sixth verse contains so express a reference to this very remarkable occurrence in David’s history, as to leave little doubt that it was the occasion on which the Psalm was composed.
it is plain that his desire is through divine grace to check and bridle his spirit, under injuries of a causeless and unprovoked description, so as not to break out into retaliation and revenge, and return evil for evil. Having attained to the exercise of forbearance, he seeks that God would judge between him and his enemies.
A Psalm of David.
Psalm 141:1-4
1. O Jehovah! I have cried unto thee, make haste unto me; give ear unto my voice when I cry unto thee. 2. Let my prayer be directed as incense before thy face; the lifting up of my hands, as
As, here and in the preceding clause, is a supplement, very properly made by our author; a word signifying like, or in the stead of, being frequently understood in the Hebrew text of the Psalms.
the evening sacrifice. 3. Set a watch, O Jehovah! upon my mouth, keep a guard upon the door of my lips. 4. Incline not my heart to an evil thing, to practice wicked works with men that work iniquity, and that I may not eat of their dainties.
 
1. O Jehovah! I have cried unto thee. From such an exordium and manner of praying, it is evident that David was laboring under no small trial, as he repeats his requests, and insists upon receiving help. Without venturing to say anything definite upon the point, we would not disapprove of the conjecture that this Psalm was written by David with reference to the persecutions he suffered from Saul. He teaches us by his example to make application immediately to God, and not be tempted, as wicked men are, to renounce prayer, and rely on other resources. He says that he cried to God, not to heaven or earth, to men or to fortune, and other vain objects, which are made mention of, in the first place at least, in such cases by the ungodly. If they do address themselves to God, it is with murmurs and complaints, howling rather than praying.

                     <ns0:p>This Psalm also must be referred to the time of <ns0:hi>Davids</ns0:hi> perse<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cution by <ns0:hi>Saul.</ns0:hi> It is an humble prayer that God would deliver him from the rage and malice of his enemies, and from those sins to which he might be inclined or provo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ked upon that occasion.</ns0:p>
                  </ns0:argument>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 LORD, I cry unto thee, make haste unto me, give ear unto my voice, when I cry unto thee.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 Let my prayer be <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> directed.</ns0:note> set forth before thee <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>Be directed to thy face.</ns0:hi> Let it not be lost, but let it come unto thee and find audience.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>as</ns0:hi> incense <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Owned and accepted by thee no less than the incense, which by thy command, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 30. 7, &c. is offered upon thine Altar, from which I am now banished and so disenabled to offer it there, and therefore I trust thou wilt accept my prayer instead of it.</ns0:note>; <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> the lifting up of my hands <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">My prayer made with hands lifted up, which was the usual gesture. See <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 11. 13. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 63. 5. & 88. 10, &c.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>as</ns0:hi> the evening sacrifice <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Which was offe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />red every evening, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 29. 39, &c. Which he mention<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> either, 1. by way of opposition to the incense which was offered in the morning: or, 2. Synecdochically, so as to include the morning-sacrifice and all the sacrifices of the day, of which this was the close; such Synecdoches being most frequent, as hath been already observed: or, 3. because the evening-sacrifice was more solemn than the morning, and was attended with more company and more prayers, whence the <ns0:hi>ninth hour,</ns0:hi> which was the time of this sacrifice, is called <ns0:hi>the hour of prayer, Acts</ns0:hi> 3. 1.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 Set a watch, O LORD, before my mouth <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">That I may not through mine own infirmity and the great provocations of mine enemies, break <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>orth into any unadvised speeches or any expressions of impa<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ience or distrust or envy or malice, &c.</ns0:note>; keep the door of my lips <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">My lips which are the door of my mouth whence words come forth.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 Incline not <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Suffer it not to be inclined or led aside either by my own errours or lusts, or by the temptations of the world or of the Devil. Thus God is frequently said <ns0:hi>to harden</ns0:hi> mens <ns0:hi>hearts</ns0:hi> not positively, for he can do no evil, nor tempt any man to it, <ns0:hi>Iam.</ns0:hi> 1. 13. but privatively, by denying sof<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ning grace.</ns0:note> my heart <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Keep me not onely from wicked speeches, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 3. but from all evil motions of my heart, which otherwise will draw me to many evil speeches and actions.</ns0:note> to <ns0:hi>any</ns0:hi> evil thing, to practise wicked works with men that work iniquity <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Either, 1. to joyn with them in their sinful courses: or, 2. to do wick<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />edly as they do.</ns0:note>: and let me not eat of their dainties <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Let me never enjoy or desire worldly comforts upon such terms as they do, to wit, with Gods wrath and curse, as instruments of wickedness, and of my own eternal destruction. My afflictions are more desirable than such prosperity. Let none of their sweet morsels, the pleasures o<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> advantages, which they gain by their wickedness, tempt me to approve of or imitate their ways.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Prov. 9. 8.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>let the righteous smi<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap> me kindly, and reprove me; let not their preci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ous oil break my head,</ns0:hi> &c.</ns0:note> Let the righteous smite me <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">To wit, with his tongue by reproofs, as the next clause explains it, which are called <ns0:hi>wounds, Prov.</ns0:hi> 27. 6. As I pray unto thee that <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> would<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>st keep me from sinful practices, so I beg it of all just men, that if I do transgress, or if, by the arts and slanders of mine enemies, any of them are made to believe that I am guilty of <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>il designs against <ns0:hi>Saul,</ns0:hi> or of any other wickedness, that they would freely admonish and reprove me for it And their reproofs shall please me better than the dainties of the wicked last mentioned, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 4.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>it shall be</ns0:hi> a kindness <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">I shall be so far from being offended with it as an act of enmity or ill will, as they may suspect, that I shall esteem it an act and sign of true friendship.</ns0:note>, and let him reprove me, <ns0:hi>it shall be</ns0:hi> an excellent oil <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Or, it shall be as <ns0:hi>the oil of the head,</ns0:hi> as it is in the Hebrew, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> which is poured upon the head, as the manner was in great feasts and solemnities.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>which</ns0:hi> shall not break my head <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Not hurt or disturb it, but on the contrary, shall heal and greatly refresh and delight it. Which is here understood by a known figure called <ns0:hi>Meiosis,</ns0:hi> whereby more is intended than is expressed, as <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 17. 21. and oft elsewhere.</ns0:note>: for yet my prayer also <ns0:hi>shall be</ns0:hi> in their calami<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ties <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Either, 1. in the calamities of those righteous persons who reproved and censured him. So this is an evidence of what he last said, that he should take their reproofs for a kindness, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause when they came into such calamities as those wherein he was involved, as all righteous men must expect sufferings at one time or other, he would not insult over them nor cen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sure them, but pity them and pray for them: or, 2. in the calamities of his enemies, of which he speaks in the next words. And so this may be added as a reason why he did so freely offer himself to the righteous to be reproved by them, if he or his cause were so bad as his enemies made them, because he was well assured that he was sincere and his cause good, and that God would bring him out of all his calamities, and bring his enemies into such calamities, that they should need and desire his prayers, which also he would willingly grant to them; and then all good men would be fully satisfied of the justice of his person and cause.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:514" />6 When their judges <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">The chief of mine enemies, their Governors Civil and Military.</ns0:note> are overthrown <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>shall be overthrown,</ns0:hi> or cast down headlong by thine exemplary vengeance. Or, as others, <ns0:hi>were left free,</ns0:hi> unhurt by me, when it was in my power to destroy them: of which see 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 24. & 26. to which histories this place is by divers learned Interpreters thought to allude. And then by <ns0:hi>their Iudges</ns0:hi> he means <ns0:hi>Saul,</ns0:hi> although he thought not fit distinctly to mention him, but onely to intimate him in an obscure and general way.</ns0:note> in stony places <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>in the hands</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>by the sides of the rock.</ns0:hi> Which may relate either, 1. to the rocky nature of those places in which <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> fell into <ns0:hi>Davids</ns0:hi> hands. See 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 24. 2. or, 2. to the ancient manner of punish<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing malefactors, which was by throwing them down from the tops of rocks: of which see 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 25. 12. or, 3. to ag<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gravate their overthrow; for falls in stony places are as most easie and frequent, so also most mischievous.</ns0:note>, they shall hear my words, for they are sweet <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Then <ns0:hi>they,</ns0:hi> either the Judges, who will be wise too late; or the people spared by my favour, when others were overthrown and war<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ned by that fearful example, <ns0:hi>will hear my words, i. e.</ns0:hi> hear<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ken to my counsels and offers which now they despise, and then <ns0:hi>they,</ns0:hi> my words, <ns0:hi>will be sweet</ns0:hi> and acceptable to them, which now they reject. Others thus, <ns0:hi>then they did hear my words that they were sweet,</ns0:hi> then they acknowledged that my words and carriage towards <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> were full of meekness and gentleness, and that I was not so false and malicious, as they had represented me to be.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 Our bones <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">My bones and the bones of my friends and followers. Our skin and flesh is in a manner consumed, and there is nothing left of us but a company of dead and dry bones. Whereby he intimates that their condition was desperate. Comp. <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 37. 11.</ns0:note> are scattered at the graves mouth <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Either, 1. literally and properly. So bar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />barously cruel were our enemies, that they not onely killed us, but left our carkasses unburied, by which means our flesh and sinews, &c. were consumed or torn in pieces by wild <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>easts, and our bones dispersed upon the face of the earth our common grave: or, if any of my followers were dead and buried, they pulled their bones out of the grave, and scattered them about: or rather, 2. Metaphorically. So the sence is, Our case is almost as hopeless as of those who are dead, and whose bones are scattered in several places.</ns0:note>, as when one cutteth and cleaveth <ns0:hi>wood</ns0:hi> upon the earth <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">As much neglected and despised by them as the chips which a Carpenter makes when he is cutting wood, which he will not stoop to take up. Or rather, as the LXX. and Chaldee and Syriack understand it, and as it is in the Hebrew, <ns0:hi>as when one</ns0:hi> (to wit, the husbandman) <ns0:hi>cutteth and cleaveth the earth</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>in the earth;</ns0:hi> which he teareth without any mercy.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 But mine eyes are unto thee, O GOD the Lord: in thee is my trust, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>make <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">

                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>. 5. 2, 3.</ns0:note> leave not my soul destitute <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>naked,</ns0:hi> as this word signifies <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 137. 7. and a<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> 
                        <ns0:hi>Aa<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>on</ns0:hi> is said to have <ns0:hi>made the people naked, Exod.</ns0:hi> 32. 25. <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> deprived of thy favour and protection. Or, <ns0:hi>do not po<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>r out my soal,</ns0:hi> to wit, unto death, as this word is used, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 53. 12.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 Keep me from <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal 140. 5. & 142. 3.</ns0:note> the snare <ns0:hi>which</ns0:hi> they have laid for me, and the grins of the workers of ini<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quity.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 Let the wicked fall into their own nets <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>Into his nets,</ns0:hi> either into Gods nets, the Relative being put without the Antecedent, as is usual in such cases, where it is easily understood. Or, each <ns0:hi>into his own nets,</ns0:hi> to wit, the mischiefs which he designs against me.</ns0:note>, whilst that I withal <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>toge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther,</ns0:hi> to wit, with my followers: or, <ns0:hi>in like manner,</ns0:hi> as I have d<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>e formerly. But this word may seem to be more fitly joyned to the <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>oregoing clause, to which it is next placed in the Hebrew, and the verse may be and is by divers both an<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cient and later Translators, thus rendred, <ns0:hi>Let the wicked fall<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                        </ns0:hi> (Or, <ns0:hi>The wicked shall fall) into their own nets together,</ns0:hi> (alto<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gether, or <ns0:hi>alik<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>,</ns0:hi> one as well as another, <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> himself not excepted, whom though I dare not destroy, God will judge) <ns0:hi>whilst that I escape,</ns0:hi> am preserved from that common calamity in which mine enemies shall perish. Which was verified by the event. For <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> was strangely kept out of harms way when <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> and others of <ns0:hi>Davids</ns0:hi> enemies were cut off by the Phisisti<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
